clue.text: Rich pastry just started at home with aid of baker

parts.note: someone rolling in it, or simply rolling, is very rich

indicators.note: only the opening of the word pastry has begun, so its first letter is taken

parts.note: in means at home, as in 'staying in tonight'

explanation.surface: A recipe note: a rich pastry has only just been started at home with a baker's help.
explanation.definitionFit: Bakers flatten dough with this wooden cylinder, so it is a classic tool of the trade.

clue.text: Getting right on top, prince allowed to follow opera

indicators.note: the R at the end of the prince's name climbs to the front, so the final letter moves to the start

parts.note: Prince Igor is Borodin's operatic hero, so prince gives his name
let means allowed, as in 'let them go'

explanation.surface: Advice to a royal on how to come out ahead before a night at the opera.
explanation.walkthrough: The R jumps from the end of Borodin's prince to the front; 'to follow' is a charade signal, so the allowing word and the literal 'to' come after.
explanation.definitionFit: Verdi's tragedy about a hunchbacked court jester is one of the best-known Italian operas.

clue.text: I'm amused by fat follower of Wycliffe

parts.note: LOL, laughing out loud, is the texting shorthand for being amused
lard is pig fat used in cooking

explanation.surface: A medieval scholar laughs at a stout disciple of the reformer John Wycliffe.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lollards were the fourteenth-century English religious reformers inspired by John Wycliffe's teaching.

clue.text: Starboard side of boat grabbed by people swimming

indicators.note: one piece is seized and held inside the other, so it sits within it

parts.note: a nation is a people

indicators.note: starboard is the right-hand side, so the right-hand half of the word boat is taken

explanation.surface: A nautical mishap: part of a boat is seized by people out swimming.
explanation.walkthrough: Starboard is a ship's right side, so the right-hand half of 'boat' is meant, not a single last letter; it sits just after the first letter of the people.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the formal Latin-derived noun for the act or sport of moving through water by stroke.

clue.text: Heroic prisoner breaking out, having seized a wagon

indicators.note: the jumbled letters take hold of the single letter and hold it inside
the words heroic prisoner break apart and reform, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A brave convict escapes from jail and grabs a wagon as a getaway vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking out' looks like the prisoner's escape but signals the rearrangement; 'having seized' puts the article inside the scrambled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: American pioneers crossed the plains in this covered wagon, its white canvas likened to a ship's sails.

clue.text: Where Quisling was certainly not embracing resistance

indicators.note: the outer phrase wraps its arms around the letter, holding it inside

parts.note: no way is an emphatic refusal, meaning certainly not
R is the physics symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: A remark that a wartime collaborator was certainly no friend of the resistance movement.
explanation.walkthrough: Vidkun Quisling led the Nazi puppet government in his home country during the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: Quisling was the Norwegian collaborator who headed the government of his occupied homeland.

clue.text: Musicians not allowed in audition

indicators.note: audition means hearing, so the word is identified by how it is pronounced

parts.note: banned means not allowed, forbidden

explanation.surface: A group of players is turned away from a tryout for a gig.
explanation.definitionFit: A band is a group of musicians playing together, so the collective plural fits.

clue.text: Police reportedly not interested in hoarding

parts.note: the Bill, or Old Bill, is British slang for the police

indicators.note: reportedly signals that the next word is identified by how it is pronounced

parts.note: bored means not interested, uninvolved

explanation.surface: Officers are said to be indifferent to someone who stockpiles goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hoarding' pretends to be stockpiling; it is the British word for a big advertising board beside a road.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a hoarding is the large outdoor panel that carries posters, the American term being the answer.

clue.text: Breathtaking channel under a bridge

parts.note: the bridge is that of the nose, and the channel beneath takes in breath, not a river under a span

explanation.surface: A stunning waterway flowing beneath an arched bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breathtaking' looks like stunning scenery, but it literally means drawing in air; the bridge is the bony ridge of the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: The nasal opening sits below the nose's bridge and is the passage through which air is inhaled.

clue.text: Barbarian in gaol arranged place of execution

indicators.note: the barbarian is placed within the rearranged letters
the letters of gaol are set out in a new order

parts.note: the Goths were Germanic tribes regarded by Rome as barbarians

explanation.surface: A savage held in a prison is set up for execution.
explanation.walkthrough: Gaol is the British spelling of jail; once rearranged, the barbarian tribe sits inside it before the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Golgotha is the hill outside Jerusalem where the crucifixion took place, also called Calvary.

clue.text: Minstrel is hired to provide enjoyment

indicators.note: the run of words supplies the answer from within itself, its letters straddling the word breaks

explanation.surface: A wandering singer is engaged to entertain the guests.
explanation.definitionFit: Relish is keen pleasure or gusto, as in eating with relish.

clue.text: Role at Stratford as writer of comic verse

definitions.meaning: Edward ... wrote nonsense verse and limericks such as The Owl and the Pussycat

explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to Shakespeare's old king and to the Victorian nonsense poet Edward.

clue.text: Study cake eaten by the poor

indicators.note: the pieces are swallowed inside the outer word

parts.note: to read a subject at university is to study it
a cake of soap is a bar of it

explanation.surface: A scholar's cake is devoured by hungry people.
explanation.walkthrough: A cake of soap is a bar, which is the sense to see; the study word and the cake word go together inside 'the', just before its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Threadbare means worn thin and shabby, so by extension poor or meagre.

clue.text: Maritime feature associated with port helped through a critical period

parts.note: the tide is the sea's regular rise and fall
Dover is the English Channel ferry port in Kent

explanation.surface: A sea phenomenon linked to a harbour town.
explanation.definitionFit: To tide someone over is an idiom for helping them through a short-term difficulty.

clue.text: Oriental lost as friend for ever

indicators.note: the word as goes missing from the longer word, so those letters are removed

parts.note: oriental means eastern, from the Orient
taken as written, the two letters being dropped
an ally is a friend or supporter

explanation.surface: An eastern companion who has gone astray, remembered fondly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lost' removes the A and S from EASTERN, leaving ETERN; 'as' looks like a link but is what is removed.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb meaning everlastingly or without end is a direct synonym of the phrase.

clue.text: What's inside German city? Stalks!

indicators.note: only the inner letters of the word are kept, its outer ones dropped

parts.note: Ulm is a city on the Danube in Germany

explanation.surface: A quizmaster asks what lies within a German city, and answers: stalks!
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' takes HA from the middle of WHAT; the 's is a link meaning 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Haulm is the collective name for the stalks or stems of crops such as peas and potatoes.

clue.text: Notts town where woman's work is never done?

definitions.meaning: A town in Nottinghamshire, an English county

definitions.text: where woman's work is never done?
definitions.meaning: split as ..., it is male territory where a woman would not work

explanation.definitionFit: Read in two parts the town's name suggests a domain reserved for men, playing on the proverb about women's work.

clue.text: Foolish person to reveal bottom part of leg

parts.note: to moon is to expose one's backside as a prank
the calf is the back of the lower leg

explanation.surface: A prankster flashes their rear and a bit of leg.
explanation.definitionFit: A mooncalf is an old word for a dolt or simpleton, once thought to be moonstruck.

clue.text: Hesitation expressed after striking part of target

indicators.note: the hesitation sound is placed after the word for striking

parts.note: workers out are on strike
er is the sound of someone hesitating

explanation.surface: An archer's hesitant noise after hitting a section of the board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'striking' looks like hitting, but it means on strike: workers who are out.
explanation.definitionFit: On an archery target the ring outside the inner rings is called the outer.

clue.text: Introduce sun and heir? That must be wrong!

indicators.note: the exclamation says the letters are wrongly ordered, so they must be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone baffled at being asked to present a sun and an heir together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That must be wrong!' rearranges SUN and HEIR; 'and' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To usher in is an idiom for introducing or heralding the start of something.

clue.text: Give in, accepting old instrument

parts.note: to accord is to grant or give, as in according someone respect

indicators.note: the outer word takes the letter in and holds it

explanation.surface: A player yields, agreeing to take on an antique musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give in' looks like surrender, but GIVE gives ACCORD and IN surrounds O.
explanation.definitionFit: The squeezebox with bellows and keys is a musical instrument.

clue.text: Rough one succeeding, entertaining centre of attraction

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to take them in, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: next means following or succeeding

indicators.note: the middle two letters of the word attraction are taken

explanation.surface: A clumsy performer wins through, amusing the star turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'centre of attraction' looks like the star of the show, but it means the two middle letters of the ten-letter word attraction.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough estimate is approximate, not precise, so rough means imprecise here.

clue.text: Congress and state legislature initially upset cats

indicators.note: in a down clue upset turns the whole run upside down, so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: congress can mean sexual intercourse
NY is the abbreviation for New York state

indicators.note: only the first letter of the word legislature is taken

explanation.surface: Politics in Washington and a state assembly overturn rules about felines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Congress' pretends to be the US legislature; 'upset' turns SEXNYL upwards to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lynxes are wild cats with tufted ears and short tails.

clue.text: Sea air won't wound deprived area

parts.note: a shanty is a sailors' work song, an air of the sea

indicators.note: wound, from wind, means twisted round, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sailor's song will not cause any injury in a poor neighbourhood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wound' looks like an injury but is the past of wind, twisting WONT into TOWN.
explanation.definitionFit: A shantytown is a settlement of crude shacks on a city's edge, a deprived area.

clue.text: Recalling Edward Elgar for starters: "Where Corals Lie"?

indicators.note: the opening letters of the words before it are taken as the first course

explanation.surface: Remembering that Edward Elgar wrote the song 'Where Corals Lie', from his Sea Pictures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' looks like part of the phrase 'for starters', but it is the fourth word whose first letter is taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Coral grows in ridges just below the sea surface, so a coral formation is where coral lies.

clue.text: Expert, almost sixty, going on and on

parts.note: a pro is a professional, an expert
in Roman numerals LIX is fifty-nine, a whole numeral for 'almost sixty', not a word cut short

explanation.surface: A skilled veteran nearing sixty who never stops talking.
explanation.definitionFit: Prolix describes speech or writing that is tediously long and wordy.

clue.text: High wind in Jamaica finally whirled general round

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go round the single letter, enclosing it
the letters of general are spun into a new order
only the last letter of Jamaica is used

explanation.surface: A storm in the Caribbean spins a commanding officer around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'whirled' turns GENERAL into NERGALE, and 'round' puts the A from Jamaica inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: On the Beaufort scale force seven is named this, one step short of a full gale.

clue.text: Girl's first to quit motor racing

indicators.note: the opening letter departs from the name

parts.note: Cindy is a girl's name; the 's is a link meaning 'has'

explanation.surface: A young woman is the first to give up motorsport.
explanation.definitionFit: IndyCar is American open-wheel racing, known as Indy after the Indianapolis 500.

clue.text: Running to and fro, suede is unlikely to slip

indicators.note: the letters run around and settle in a new order

explanation.surface: Dashing back and forth in suede shoes, you won't lose your footing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Running' rearranges TO, FRO and SUEDE; 'and' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone surefooted keeps their balance and is not likely to stumble.
